# Who is on the other side?

*You'll need fills and passive orders (chapter 2), and half the spread against the impact (chapter 4). Fill models
and grids are named here and explained in chapters 6 and 7.*

## The story

Everything in the template was tuned on Prosperity data. So we took it, unchanged, into ABIDES, an independent market
simulator whose traders include a hundred "value" agents with noisy private views of a hidden price, and momentum
traders who follow moves. ABIDES prices are in cents.

The template lost. Over ten days it made −21,798 cents (about −$218) under the most optimistic fill model, and
−362,428 (about −$3,624) with orders that rest. Of a 36-cell grid of its settings, none made money with resting
orders; doing nothing beat every one.

Then the test that explains it. We made twenty copies of the same ten days with each day's ticks put in a random order,
same books, same trades, no sequence, and ran a small search over the bot's quoting distance on each. On the shuffled
days the best setting made **+4,540,545 cents** on average, about +$45,000 (@fig-shuffle). On Prosperity's Kelp the
same test changes almost nothing: 27,390 credits on the real days, 27,326 on the shuffled ones [(`IDEAS.md`, "An independent generator: ABIDES's RMSC04")]{.src}.

![The grid's best PnL on the real days and on shuffled copies: ABIDES (cents, ten days) and Prosperity 3's Kelp
(credits, three days); each panel on its own scale. Data: `data/shuffle.csv`, from `arena.grid ... --permute 20`.](figures/f07_shuffle.png){#fig-shuffle
fig-alt="Two bar charts. ABIDES: minus 21,798 cents on the real days against plus 4.54 million on the shuffled ones. Kelp: 27,390 against 27,326."}

Shuffling keeps every book and every trade and destroys the sequence: *what happens after* each fill, including
moves that keep going. On ABIDES that was where the loss lived. The order of events was the adverse selection.

## The idea

### The fills you get are the ones you didn't want

A resting quote doesn't choose who trades with it. It is filled whenever someone finds it worth taking, and the people
most eager to take it are the ones who know the price is about to move through it. A bid gets hit just before the
price falls; an ask gets lifted just before it rises. This is *adverse selection*: conditional on being filled, a
market maker's fills are worse than its quotes looked.

The measurement is the *markout*, a fill's profit some ticks later:

::: {.eq speak="a fill's markout at h ticks is how far the price moved in its favour by then: the side, times the mid h ticks later less the fill's price"}
$$\text{markout}(h) = \text{side} \times \big(\text{mid}_{t+h} - \text{fill price}\big)$$
:::

with side +1 for a buy and −1 for a sell. Straight after the fill the markout of a passive fill is the edge it was quoted at, about
half the spread. On an uninformed market it stays there as h grows. Under adverse selection it falls, and if it falls
below zero the market maker pays to trade. On ABIDES our passive fills started at about +2 cents a unit; a single tick
later the price had moved about 2 cents against them, leaving about nothing, and fills against the last move lost on
every day
[(`IDEAS.md`, "An independent generator: ABIDES's RMSC04")]{.src}.

### Two kinds of market

Prosperity's products are the friendly kind. On Kelp, where we measured it, the takers look close to random: our position's correlation with where the
price went next was between −0.10 and +0.18 on Kelp, about nothing
[(`IDEAS.md`, "`skew` against Kelp's long position")]{.src}. Kelp sits long much of the day for the same reason:
more of its takers happen to sell, and the bot buys what they sell. That position is the flow, not a signal.

ABIDES is the other kind: some traders know something, and their trades move the price after them (chapter 4's
impact, +1.3 ticks within 50). The template's whole playbook, quote close to a fair value and wait, was built for the
first kind and loses on the second. The Arena may be either, or each product may be different, which is why the repo
has a test for it before anything else is tuned.

### When someone is informed, follow them

Adverse selection has a mirror image. If one trader is reliably informed, their trades are a signal. On Prosperity 3,
one trader, named Olivia once round 5 showed names, bought at or near each day's low and sold at or near its high: in
round 5 all 19 of her trades were followed by a move her way at 100, 1,000 and 5,000 ticks. Frankfurt Hedgehogs had
spotted her from trade sizes before names were shown, and traded on her signal
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Following informed counterparties"; `references/prosperity3-frankfurt-hedgehogs/README.md:270-319`)]{.src}.
Copying her on top of plain market making took our Croissants from about 2 thousand credits a day to 13 to 26 thousand.

The warning is chapter 7's story. In Prosperity 4, several teams each found a different "informed" trader, and none of
those signals survived a day they hadn't been chosen on. A real Olivia is right on every trade; a lucky one is right
for two days.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
Adverse selection is selection bias with an adversary: the sample of fills you observe is chosen by the people who
profit from your errors, so it is biased in the worst direction, and more so the more visible your quotes are. The
shuffle test is a permutation test: destroy the temporal order and see whether the result needed it. Where it differs
from the usual use: here the order costing you money is the finding, not a null to reject.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="In the repo"}
- Markouts of any run: `uv run python -m arena.analysis results/` (from `arena.backtest ... --out results/`); by
  market state, `experiments.day.quote_markouts`.
- Prosperity-like or agent-like, per product: `experiments.day.premise` (the shuffle test and the impact, together).
- Informed counterparties: `experiments.day.counterparties`; the template's `copy` mode follows named traders.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="On the day"}
`RUNBOOK.md`, "Each round", T+0:15 runs `experiments.day.premise` on the new days: whether each product is
Prosperity-like or agent-like, and which grids to run (`ON_THE_DAY.md`, "What kind of market is each product?").
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper" appearance="simple"}
- Bouchaud et al., *Trades, Quotes and Prices*, ch. 11 §11.1–11.3 (PDF pp. 227–240): the response function, the
  impact after a trade.
- DeLise, *The negative drift of a limit order fill* (28 pp.): markouts, and why a backtest's fill rule decides them.
:::
